# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Reading dashboards is Day 1; building them is how an operations team turns its knowledge into a shared view. Most dashboard work is not creating from scratch but improving an existing dashboard: changing a visualisation, adding the missing series, making it reusable with variables, calculating a field the data source does not provide, and adding thresholds so that "normal" and "bad" are visible at a glance.  
In this lab you work only in your browser, in the Grafana Cloud UI, directly inside the pre-provisioned easyTravel Overview dashboard that the whole cohort shares (or the workspace copy assigned to you in folder u\<seat\>). You have no terminal, Docker or Prometheus CLI access: all metrics are pre-collected and ingested by Grafana Alloy. You do not build or copy a dashboard. You verify the data in Explore, triage and modify the existing panels in the query editor, add p50/p99 and 4xx series with field overrides, configure service and percentile variables and chain them, calculate an error percentage with a transformation, configure thresholds, and verify the result in the dashboard JSON (Edit as code).

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can change a dashboard during an incident to show exactly what the team needs. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will make thresholds and percentiles show what "bad" looks like. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Variables make one dashboard work for every service and environment. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

A Grafana panel is a pipeline: queries → transformations → field configuration (units, overrides, thresholds) → visualisation.  
*Figure: Panel Pipeline — Data Source Queries (A, B, C) → Transformations (Merge, Add Field From Calculation, Organize, Sort) → Field Config (Unit, Min/Max, Thresholds, Overrides) → Visualisation (Time Series, Stat, Gauge, Table, Bar Chart)*

| Building Block | Where in the Editor | Example in This Lab | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Query editor | Query tab: Builder / Code, Legend, Min interval, Format | histogram\_quantile(\$percentile, …) | What data the panel gets |
| Additional series / overrides | Query B, C …; Overrides → Fields with name | p50/p99 lines; 4xx series; p99 dashed red | Compare signals in one panel |
| Variables | Dashboard settings → Variables | \$service (query), \$percentile (custom), \$route (chained) | One dashboard for many cases |
| Transformations / thresholds | Transform data tab; Field → Thresholds | Error % \= 5xx / Requests; red above 5 % | Derived fields; visible "bad" |

*Figure: Chained Variables — \$env → \$service \= label\_values(http\_server\_requests\_total{env="\$env"}, service) → \$route \= label\_values(…{env="\$env", service="\$service"}, route) → Panels Use All Three*

# 

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Work in the Shared Dashboard, Verify as Code

The easyTravel Overview dashboard is pre-provisioned in the Grafana Cloud stack by the instructor, and every learner uses the same dashboard. Its metrics arrive through Grafana Alloy, so there is nothing to install or start: you open the existing dashboard, change its panels in edit mode and save. Every change you make in the UI ends up in the dashboard JSON — panels, targets (queries), fieldConfig (units, thresholds, overrides), transformations and templating (variables). Reading that JSON in Edit → Edit as code is a quick way to prove the dashboard is built as intended, and Edit → Settings → Versions shows every saved change.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| Variables turn ten similar dashboards into one. When a new service appears, the variable lists it automatically. |
|  |
| Thresholds and overrides carry knowledge: the person on call sees red without knowing that 5 % errors or 1 s p95 is bad for this service. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Query-Side vs Grafana-Side Calculation

You can calculate in PromQL (sum(rate(…5..)) / sum(rate(…))) or in Grafana with transformations (divide two query results field by field). PromQL calculations work everywhere the query is used (alerts, other dashboards) and over any time range; transformations work only in that panel but can combine results from different queries or data sources. Prefer PromQL for metrics you alert on, transformations for presentation (tables, renaming, joining).

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake When Developing Dashboards |
| :---- |
| An engineer adds a \$service variable but forgets to use it in half of the panels — the dashboard silently mixes the selected service with all others. |
|  |
| REASON: Variables do nothing until every query references them. |
|  |
| YOU MUST search the dashboard JSON for hard-coded values after adding a variable and test each panel with two different variable values. |

## 3.3  Transformations Used in This Lab

| Transformation | Does | Configuration | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Merge | Joins rows from several queries by common labels | (none) | One table: Requests, 5xx, p95 per route |
| Add field from calculation | New column from other columns | Binary operation: 5xx errors / Requests | Error ratio per route |
| Organize fields | Rename, hide and order columns | Rename Value \#A → Requests … | Readable table |
| Sort by | Orders rows | Field: Error ratio, reverse | Worst route first |

| 📝  How to Decide Between a Variable and a New Panel |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Is it the same question for a different object (service, route, environment, percentile)?" Then use a variable. If it is a different question (latency vs saturation), add a panel. If you need the same panel once per value side by side, use panel or row repeat on the variable. |

| TASK 2 — SERIES: Latency Percentiles, 4xx and Overrides |
| :---- |

| 2 | Add Additional Metric Series to Panels and Style Them with Overrides*Grafana Dashboard Development SOP — Day 4 — Lab 2* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

You modify the existing latency panel: rename it, set its unit, and add p50 and p99 next to p95 with queries B and C on grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom using \$\_\_rate\_interval. A regex override styles every p99 line, and the error panel gets a separate 4xx series.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Queries to add (panel edit → \+ Add query) |
| ----- |
|  |
| \# Panel "p95 latency by route" (existing panel) → Edit → rename "Latency percentiles by route" · Standard options → Unit: seconds (s), Decimals 2  |
| \#   B (legend "p50 {{route}}"): |
| histogram\_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, route) (rate(http\_server\_request\_duration\_seconds\_bucket{env="\$env",service="easytravel-frontend",route=\~"\$route"}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\]))) ![][image8] |
| \#   C (legend "p99 {{route}}"): |
| histogram\_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route) (rate(http\_server\_request\_duration\_seconds\_bucket{env="\$env",service="easytravel-frontend",route=\~"\$route"}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])))  |
| \#   Overrides → Fields with name matching regex  p99.\*  → Line style: Dashes · Color: red ![][image9]  |
|  |
| \# Panel "5xx error ratio by route" (existing panel) → rename "Error ratio by route (4xx / 5xx)"; set legend of A to "5xx {{route}}"  |
| \#   B (legend "4xx {{route}}"): |
| sum by (route) (rate(http\_server\_requests\_total{env="\$env",service="easytravel-frontend",route=\~"\$route",status=\~"4.."}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])) or sum by (route) (rate(http\_server\_requests\_total{env="\$env",service="easytravel-frontend",route=\~"\$route"}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])) \* 0 ![][image10] |
|  |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Latency panel: three lines per route (p50 \< p95 ≤ p99); p99 lines dashed red |
|  |
| **2.A  Why are p95 and p99 almost the same for checkout when healthy (hint: histogram buckets)?**  Answer: Histogram buckets have limited resolution: p95 and p99 can fall into the same bucket, so the two lines are close or identical. The result is only as precise as the bucket bounds. |
| **2.B  What is the advantage of a regex override (p99.\*) over one override per series?**  Answer: One regex override styles every matching p99 series, including routes that appear later, without one override per series. |

| ⌨  Task 4 — Table transformations, thresholds, Edit as code check |
| ----- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: Panel "Route summary (selected time range)" → Transform data (existing: Merge, Organize fields) → \+ Add transformation: ![][image13] |
| \#   Add field from calculation · Mode: Binary operation · "5xx errors" / "Requests" · Alias "Error ratio"   |
| \#   Sort by · Field: Error ratio · Replace all fields: on  |
| \#   Overrides → Fields with name "Error ratio" → Unit: Percent (0.0-1.0) · Cell type: Colored text · Thresholds: green, 0.01 orange, 0.05 red  |
|  |
| \# Step 2: Thresholds |
| \#   "Latency percentiles by route": Thresholds base green, 1 red · Show thresholds: As lines (dashed) ![][image14]  |
| \#   "Requests / s (now)": Thresholds base green; Color mode: Background solid (no red — traffic alone is not bad) ![][image15]  |
| \#   Save dashboard → add a change note (e.g. "u\<seat\>: Task 4") → Save ![][image16] |
|  |
|   |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: table with Requests, 5xx errors, p95 (s), Error ratio — the failing route first while or after cue C1 has run, others near 0 % |
| Step 3: templating names env · route · service · percentile  (in your order) |
|         Route summary panel transformations: \["merge","organize","calculateField","sortBy"\] |
| **4.A  Would you calculate the error ratio in PromQL or with a transformation for an alert? For this table? Why?**  Answer: For an alert: calculate the error ratio directly in PromQL (e.g. sum by (route) (rate(http\_server\_requests\_total{status=\~"5.."}\[5m\])) / sum by (route) (rate(http\_server\_requests\_total\[5m\]))). Grafana transformations run only in the browser when the panel renders and are not evaluated by alert rules; an alert rule needs a single server-side PromQL expression that is evaluated on a schedule even when no dashboard is open.For this table: a transformation (Add field from calculation → Binary operation 5xx errors / Requests) is ideal because the table already queries the Requests and 5xx errors counts for display. Deriving the ratio in the panel avoids a duplicate Prometheus query and keeps the percentage consistent with the numbers in the adjacent columns. |
| **4.B  Why should a traffic stat not turn red? Which panels deserve thresholds and why?**  Answer: •  Why a traffic stat (Requests / s (now)) should not turn red: high traffic by itself is not an error or degradation — it can be normal peak usage, a campaign or organic growth. Turning a pure throughput panel red causes false alarms and alert fatigue while the system is healthy.•  Which panels deserve thresholds: Error ratio by route (4xx / 5xx) and the Route summary Error ratio column (0.01 orange / 0.05 red), because elevated error percentages are user-facing failures (such as HTTP 500 checkouts); p95 latency (now) and Latency percentiles by route (1 s red), because high tail latency signals degradation, saturation or downstream bottlenecks that users feel. |

# 

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Save button missing or "You do not have permission" | Viewer role on the shared folder | Profile → your role; folder permissions | Ask the instructor for Editor on easyTravel (shared) — do not use Save as copy |
| Service variable empty | Wrong data source or \$env not set | Variable editor → Preview of values | Select grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom; Environment \= cohort |
| Panels show "No data" after adding \$service | Quote or label typo (service="\$service") | Query inspector → Query | Fix the selector; check variable value |
| \$percentile shows as text in title only | Variable not used in expr | Inspect the query | histogram\_quantile(\$percentile, …) |
| Calculated field missing | Column names differ (renamed before/after) | Table view → Debug transformations | Use the names after "Organize fields" or reorder transformations |
| "Someone else has updated this dashboard" | Another learner saved the shared dashboard first | Save dialog shows the conflict warning | Do not overwrite — copy your panel JSON, reload, reapply your change and save |
| Panel query works but Explore shows "No data" | Template variables (\$env, \$service, \$route) are not defined in Explore | Query inspector shows the resolved query | Use real labels env="cohort", service="easytravel-frontend" |
| Explore shows no metrics at all | Wrong data source (-logs or \-traces) selected | Data source picker in Explore | Select grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom and Code mode |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Panel Pipeline |
| :---- |
| Without notes: describe the order queries → transformations → field config → visualisation. |
| Where did each of your changes live in the JSON? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: targets, transformations, fieldConfig (defaults, overrides), options/type. |
| **Discussion 2 — Series and Overrides** |
| What did p50/p95/p99 together show that p95 alone did not? |
| When are too many series a problem? |
|  |
| Key insight: the spread between percentiles shows how uneven latency is; keep panels readable (few, labelled series). |
| **Discussion 3 — Variables** |
| Which other variables would make this dashboard more useful (instance, interval, data source)? |
| What are the risks of All \+ regex variables on big data? |
|  |
| Key answer: data source and interval variables are common; All can create heavy queries. |
| **Discussion 4 — Transformations vs PromQL** |
| Which of today's calculations belong in PromQL, which in Grafana? |
| How do you review dashboard changes in a team (JSON in Git, provisioning)? |
|  |
| Answer: alerting logic in PromQL/recording rules; presentation in transformations; store reviewed JSON in Git and provision it. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Saving over another learner's change | Many learners edit one shared dashboard | Lost panel changes | Reload on conflict; never Save and overwrite |
| Variables not used everywhere | Many panels to edit | Mixed data | Search JSON for hard-coded values |
| Variables copied into Explore | Panel queries pasted as they are | "No data" in Explore | Replace variables with real label values |
| Thresholds on everything | Colour looks helpful | Alarm fatigue on dashboards | Thresholds only where values can be bad |
| Unlabelled extra series | Default legends | Confusing lines | Custom legends and overrides |
| Transformations for alert logic | Quick in UI | Alerts cannot use them | Calculate in PromQL / recording rules |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — GRAFANA DASHBOARD DEVELOPMENT COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Open | Dashboards → easyTravel (shared) → easyTravel Overview → Edit | Work in place |
| Query editor | Builder / Code · Legend {{label}} · Format | Per query |
| Inspector | Panel ⋮ → Inspect → Query / Data / JSON | Debug |
| More series | \+ Add query (B, C …) | Same panel |
| Override | Overrides → Fields with name matching regex | Style one series |
| Query variable | label\_values(metric{env="\$env"}, service) | Dynamic list |
| Custom variable | 0.5,0.9,0.95,0.99 | Fixed list |
| Chained | …{service="\$service"} | Depends on another |
| Calculated field | Add field from calculation → Binary operation | Transformation |
| Thresholds | Field → Thresholds; Show thresholds: As lines | Visible "bad" |
| Dashboard JSON | Edit → Edit as code (JSON model) | Verify as code |
| Versions | Edit → Settings → Versions | See and restore changes |
| Explore | Explore → grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom → Code | Check data flow |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — learners have no terminal or backend access. Do this once in the Grafana Cloud stack (e.g. broaddinghy3089.grafana.net), at least 30 minutes before the cohort.  
1\. Metric ingestion: Grafana Alloy on the easyTravel environment must ingest http\_server\_requests\_total{env="cohort",service,route,status} and http\_server\_request\_duration\_seconds\_bucket with the same labels, for services easytravel-frontend and easytravel-backend, with at least a checkout route. Check once in Explore on grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom with count by (service, route) (http\_server\_requests\_total{env="cohort"}).  
2\. Shared dashboard: the "easyTravel Overview" dashboard is pre-provisioned in the folder "easyTravel (shared)" with all panels and variables using grafanacloud-\<stack\>-prom. Its variable is env (custom, default cohort); its panels are exactly those named in Tasks 1–4. If you assign learners a workspace copy in folder u\<seat\>, have it in place before class and tell each learner which one to use.  
3\. Permissions: learners need the Editor permission on the shared folder (or on their assigned workspace). They must not have Admin rights or access to data-source, Alloy or user settings.  
4\. Fault cues: C1 at about T+14 (Task 2\) — announce "CreditCardCheckError500 ON" and the time, then switch the fault on in easyTravel. C2 about 4 minutes later, before Task 3 — announce "OFF" and the time, then switch it off.  
5\. Shared editing: remind learners to add a change note on every save and to reload instead of overwriting when Grafana reports a conflict. Edit → Settings → Versions lets you restore an earlier version if a panel is broken.  
6\. At the end of the lab confirm the fault is OFF and keep the dashboard as the learners left it — Labs 3–5 reuse it.
